claim: Acute phase reactants (APRs) are secretory proteins exhibiting large expression changes in response to proinflammatory cytokines.
source: Acute phase reactants (APRs) are secretory proteins exhibiting large expression changes in response to proinflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about APRs that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: The expression pattern of C-reactive protein (CRP) is causally determined by DNMT3A and TET2-tuned promoter methylation status.
source: Here we show that the expression pattern of a major human APR, that is C-reactive protein (CRP), is casually determined by DNMT3A and TET2-tuned promoter methylation status.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental manipulations of DNMT3A and TET2 shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: CRP features a CpG-poor promoter with its CpG motifs located in binding sites of STAT3, C/EBP-β and NF-κB.
source: CRP features a CpG-poor promoter with its CpG motifs located in binding sites of STAT3, C/EBP-β and NF-κB.
evidence: This is supported by the schematic illustration in Figure 1A showing the locations of CpG motifs and transcription factor binding sites.

claim: CRP promoter CpG motifs are highly methylated at the resting state.
source: These motifs are highly methylated at the resting state, but undergo STAT3- and NF-κB-dependent demethylation upon cytokine stimulation, leading to markedly enhanced recruitment of C/EBP-β that boosts CRP expression.
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: CRP promoter CpG motifs undergo STAT3- and NF-κB-dependent demethylation upon cytokine stimulation.
source: These motifs are highly methylated at the resting state, but undergo STAT3- and NF-κB-dependent demethylation upon cytokine stimulation, leading to markedly enhanced recruitment of C/EBP-β that boosts CRP expression.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that STAT3 and NF-κB inhibition affects promoter methylation (Figure 2B, 2C, 5F).

claim: Cytokine-induced demethylation of CRP promoter leads to markedly enhanced recruitment of C/EBP-β that boosts CRP expression.
source: These motifs are highly methylated at the resting state, but undergo STAT3- and NF-κB-dependent demethylation upon cytokine stimulation, leading to markedly enhanced recruitment of C/EBP-β that boosts CRP expression.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 4A showing enhanced C/EBP-β recruitment upon induction, and by experiments showing C/EBP-β is the major effector (Figure 5J, 5K).

claim: Withdrawal of cytokines results in a rapid recovery of promoter methylation and termination of CRP induction.
source: Withdrawal of cytokines, by contrast, results in a rapid recovery of promoter methylation and termination of CRP induction.
evidence: This is supported by the time course data in Figure 1G showing recovery of both methylation and expression after cytokine washout.

claim: Reversible methylation regulates the expression of highly inducible genes carrying CpG-poor promoters with APRs as representatives.
source: Further analysis suggests that reversible methylation also regulates the expression of highly inducible genes carrying CpG-poor promoters with APRs as representatives.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6 and 7 showing similar patterns for SAA and genome-wide analysis of CpG-poor promoters.

claim: APRs are liver-produced plasma proteins constituting an integral part of innate defense.
source: Acute phase reactants (APRs) are liver-produced plasma proteins constituting an integral part of innate defense (Gabay and Kushner, 1999; Medzhitov, 2007).
evidence: This is a well-established fact supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: APRs are defined by a substantial change (>25%) of their plasma concentrations in response to inflammation.
source: They are defined by a substantial change (>25%) of their plasma concentrations in response to inflammation.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: IL-6 and IL-1β are chief inducers of APR expression through activation of STAT3, NF-κB and C/EBP in hepatocytes.
source: IL-6 (Kopf et al., 1994) and IL-1β (Zheng et al., 1995) are chief inducers of APR expression through activation of STAT3, NF-κB and C/EBP in hepatocytes (Bode et al., 2012; Quinton et al., 2012; Poli, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: CRP plasma concentrations at baseline are less than 2–3 µg/ml.
source: C-reactive protein (CRP) is the first APR to be discovered, whose plasma concentrations at baseline are less than 2–3 µg/ml, but can rapidly increase up to 1000-fold upon infection or tissue injury; the heightened levels of CRP, however, return to the baseline with the resolution of inflammation (Pepys and Hirschfield, 2003; Du Clos, 2013; Pathak and Agrawal, 2019).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CRP supported by citations.

claim: CRP plasma concentrations can rapidly increase up to 1000-fold upon infection or tissue injury.
source: C-reactive protein (CRP) is the first APR to be discovered, whose plasma concentrations at baseline are less than 2–3 µg/ml, but can rapidly increase up to 1000-fold upon infection or tissue injury; the heightened levels of CRP, however, return to the baseline with the resolution of inflammation (Pepys and Hirschfield, 2003; Du Clos, 2013; Pathak and Agrawal, 2019).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CRP supported by citations.

claim: Heightened levels of CRP return to baseline with the resolution of inflammation.
source: C-reactive protein (CRP) is the first APR to be discovered, whose plasma concentrations at baseline are less than 2–3 µg/ml, but can rapidly increase up to 1000-fold upon infection or tissue injury; the heightened levels of CRP, however, return to the baseline with the resolution of inflammation (Pepys and Hirschfield, 2003; Du Clos, 2013; Pathak and Agrawal, 2019).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CRP supported by citations.

claim: A region of ~220 bp in the proximal promoter of CRP contains binding sites for STAT3, NF-κB and C/EBP-β and is sufficient to mediate CRP induction by IL-6 and IL-1β.
source: A region of ~220 bp in the proximal promoter of CRP that contains (nonconical) binding sites for STAT3, NF-κB and C/EBP-β is identified to be sufficient to mediate CRP induction by IL-6 and IL-1β (Singh et al., 2007; Young et al., 2008; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by previous studies cited and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The promoter SNP rs3091244 is associated with plasma levels of CRP.
source: Intriguingly, a promoter SNP (rs3091244) associated with plasma levels of CRP is located at 286 bp upstream the transcription start site (Szalai et al., 2005; Zacho et al., 2008; Allin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genetic association studies.

claim: The SNP rs3091244 is located at 286 bp upstream the transcription start site of CRP.
source: Intriguingly, a promoter SNP (rs3091244) associated with plasma levels of CRP is located at 286 bp upstream the transcription start site (Szalai et al., 2005; Zacho et al., 2008; Allin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the location of the SNP supported by citations.

claim: The SNP rs3091244 does not exist in binding sites of transcription factors critical to CRP expression.
source: This SNP does not exist in binding sites of transcription factors (TFs) critical to CRP expression.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the promoter sequence and TF binding sites shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The major −286C allele of rs3091244 constitutes a CpG motif at which DNA methylation frequently occurs.
source: Rather, the major −286C allele constitutes a CpG motif, at which DNA methylation frequently occurs; whereas the minor alleles of −286A/T disrupt the CpG motif and are associated with enhanced CRP expression.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and the known properties of CpG motifs.

claim: The minor alleles of rs3091244 (−286A/T) disrupt the CpG motif and are associated with enhanced CRP expression.
source: Rather, the major −286C allele constitutes a CpG motif, at which DNA methylation frequently occurs; whereas the minor alleles of −286A/T disrupt the CpG motif and are associated with enhanced CRP expression.
evidence: This is supported by the allele-specific methylation data in Figure 1F and previous genetic association studies.

claim: There are only four additional CpGs within the proximal promoter of CRP besides the −286CpG.
source: Beside the −286CpG, there are only four additional CpGs within the proximal promoter of CRP.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the CRP promoter shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Two CpGs in the CRP promoter are located at the binding sites of STAT3 and NF-κB/C/EBP-β.
source: Importantly, two of those CpGs are located at the binding sites of STAT3 and NF-κB/C/EBP-β (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the schematic diagram in Figure 1A.

claim: Promoter methylation affects TF recruitment.
source: Given that promoter methylation affects TF recruitment (Hu et al., 2013; Yin et al., 2017) and contributes to gene silencing (Jones, 2012; Wu and Zhang, 2014; Dor and Cedar, 2018; Luo et al., 2018; Blattler and Farnham, 2013), it is notable that levels of promoter methylation and expression of CRP appear to be negatively associated albeit with undefined causality (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Promoter methylation contributes to gene silencing.
source: Given that promoter methylation affects TF recruitment (Hu et al., 2013; Yin et al., 2017) and contributes to gene silencing (Jones, 2012; Wu and Zhang, 2014; Dor and Cedar, 2018; Luo et al., 2018; Blattler and Farnham, 2013), it is notable that levels of promoter methylation and expression of CRP appear to be negatively associated albeit with undefined causality (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Levels of promoter methylation and expression of CRP appear to be negatively associated.
source: Given that promoter methylation affects TF recruitment (Hu et al., 2013; Yin et al., 2017) and contributes to gene silencing (Jones, 2012; Wu and Zhang, 2014; Dor and Cedar, 2018; Luo et al., 2018; Blattler and Farnham, 2013), it is notable that levels of promoter methylation and expression of CRP appear to be negatively associated albeit with undefined causality (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and data in the current study.

claim: Methylation levels of CRP promoter in normal liver tissues are much lower than in other tissues.
source: Accordingly, methylation levels of CRP promoter in normal liver tissues were much lower than that in other tissues (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: CRP is expressed predominantly by the liver.
source: CRP is expressed predominantly, if not solely, by the liver (Pepys and Hirschfield, 2003; Du Clos, 2013).
evidence: This is a well-established fact supported by citations.

claim: CRP promoter is most demethylated in the liver compared to other human tissues.
source: Analysis of published bisulfite sequencing datasets also confirmed that CRP promoter was most demethylated in the liver (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published datasets shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CRP exhibits a comparable expression pattern in rabbits as in humans.
source: Similar results were further obtained in rabbits (Figure 1D), wherein CRP exhibits a comparable expression pattern as in humans.
evidence: This is supported by the rabbit tissue data in Figure 1D.

claim: Malignant liver tissues express more CRP than adjacent normal tissues.
source: Moreover, malignant liver tissues expressed more CRP than adjacent normal tissues, and they were also less methylated at CRP promoter (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the tumor vs. normal tissue comparison data in Figure 1E.

claim: Malignant liver tissues are less methylated at CRP promoter than adjacent normal tissues.
source: Moreover, malignant liver tissues expressed more CRP than adjacent normal tissues, and they were also less methylated at CRP promoter (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the tumor vs. normal tissue comparison data in Figure 1E.

claim: There is an inverse association between levels of promoter methylation and CRP expression across different tissues or cell types.
source: These data together reveal an inverse association between levels of promoter methylation and CRP expression across different tissues or cell types.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figures 1B-E.

claim: Hep3B cells harbor distinct alleles at the −286 position of CRP promoter, with −286C on one allele and −286A on the other.
source: CRP promoter in Hep3B cells harbors distinct alleles at the −286 position, with −286C on one allele and −286A on the other.
evidence: This is supported by the allele-specific sequencing data in Figure 1F.

claim: All promoter CpGs on the −286A allele are much less methylated than on the −286C allele at the resting state in Hep3B cells.
source: Intriguingly, in addition to lacking the −286CpG, all other promoter CpGs on the −286A allele were much less methylated than that on the −286C allele at the resting state (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the allele-specific methylation data in Figure 1F.

claim: The allelic imbalance of promoter methylation is reinforced at the induced state.
source: Such an allelic imbalance of promoter methylation was further reinforced at the induced state.
evidence: This is supported by the allele-specific methylation data in Figure 1F comparing resting and induced states.

claim: The induction of CRP by IL-6 and IL-1β is accompanied by prominent promoter demethylation.
source: Notably, the induction of CRP by IL-6 and IL-1β was accompanied by prominent promoter demethylation (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the time course data in Figure 1G.

claim: Following washout of cytokines, both the expression and the promoter methylation of CRP are rapidly recovered.
source: Following washout of the cytokines, however, both the expression and the promoter methylation of CRP were rapidly recovered.
evidence: This is supported by the washout time course data in Figure 1G.

claim: The methylation level of a 5' UTR CpG of CRP remains constant during cytokine treatment and washout.
source: By contrast, the methylation level of a 5' UTR CpG remained constant during the entire time course.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1G showing specificity of the methylation changes to the promoter region.

claim: Levels of promoter methylation and CRP expression are specifically and dynamically associated in the same cell type.
source: Therefore, levels of promoter methylation and CRP expression are also specifically and dynamically associated in the same cell type.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the time course data in Figure 1G.

claim: Treating Hep3B cells with 5-aza or RG108 significantly enhances CRP expression at the resting state.
source: Treating Hep3B cells with 5-aza or RG108 to inhibit DNA methylation significantly enhanced CRP expression at the resting state, but showed little effect at the induced state (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) wherein CRP promoter also underwent active demethylation (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: 5-aza and RG108 show little effect on CRP expression at the induced state.
source: Treating Hep3B cells with 5-aza or RG108 to inhibit DNA methylation significantly enhanced CRP expression at the resting state, but showed little effect at the induced state (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) wherein CRP promoter also underwent active demethylation (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: 5-aza can moderately rescue the induced expression of CRP when STAT3 is inhibited.
source: Nevertheless, 5-aza could moderately rescue the induced expression of CRP when STAT3 or NF-κB was inhibited (Figure 2B and C), hinting for their involvement in active demethylation of CRP promoter.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: 5-aza can moderately rescue the induced expression of CRP when NF-κB is inhibited.
source: Nevertheless, 5-aza could moderately rescue the induced expression of CRP when STAT3 or NF-κB was inhibited (Figure 2B and C), hinting for their involvement in active demethylation of CRP promoter.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: STAT3 and NF-κB are involved in active demethylation of CRP promoter.
source: Nevertheless, 5-aza could moderately rescue the induced expression of CRP when STAT3 or NF-κB was inhibited (Figure 2B and C), hinting for their involvement in active demethylation of CRP promoter.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with 5-aza shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: In vitro methylation before transfection markedly suppresses the reporter activity of CRP promoter in Hep3B cells.
source: Moreover, in vitro methylation before transfection markedly suppressed the reporter activity of CRP promoter in Hep3B cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 2D.

claim: The suppression of CRP promoter activity by methylation is partially reversed by mutating individual CpG motifs.
source: This suppression, however, was partially reversed by mutating individual CpG motifs, and was completely absent with a CpG-null mutant of CRP promoter.
evidence: This is supported by the luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 2D.

claim: The suppression of CRP promoter activity by methylation is completely absent with a CpG-null mutant.
source: This suppression, however, was partially reversed by mutating individual CpG motifs, and was completely absent with a CpG-null mutant of CRP promoter.
evidence: This is supported by the luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 2D.

claim: Promoter methylation inhibits CRP expression.
source: These results suggest that promoter methylation inhibits, whereas its demethylation enhances CRP expression, thus supporting a causal association.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figure 2.

claim: Promoter demethylation enhances CRP expression.
source: These results suggest that promoter methylation inhibits, whereas its demethylation enhances CRP expression, thus supporting a causal association.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figure 2.

claim: CpG methylation is mediated by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs).
source: CpG methylation and demethylation are mediated by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) and ten-eleven translocations (TETs), respectively (Jones, 2012; Wu and Zhang, 2014; Dor and Cedar, 2018; Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CpG demethylation is mediated by ten-eleven translocations (TETs).
source: CpG methylation and demethylation are mediated by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) and ten-eleven translocations (TETs), respectively (Jones, 2012; Wu and Zhang, 2014; Dor and Cedar, 2018; Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Knockdown of DNMT3A enhances CRP expression in Hep3B cells.
source: Indeed, RNAi screening revealed that knockdown (KD) of DNMT3A enhanced (Figure 3A), whereas KD of TET2 reduced CRP expression in Hep3B cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi screening data in Figure 3A.

claim: Knockdown of TET2 reduces CRP expression in Hep3B cells.
source: Indeed, RNAi screening revealed that knockdown (KD) of DNMT3A enhanced (Figure 3A), whereas KD of TET2 reduced CRP expression in Hep3B cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi screening data in Figure 3B.

claim: Knockout of DNMT3A enhances CRP expression with more pronounced effects than knockdown.
source: Knockout (KO) of DNMT3A (Figure 3C) or TET2 (Figure 3D) with Cas9 yielded consistent but more pronounced effects.
evidence: This is supported by the Cas9 knockout data in Figure 3C.

claim: Knockout of TET2 reduces CRP expression with more pronounced effects than knockdown.
source: Knockout (KO) of DNMT3A (Figure 3C) or TET2 (Figure 3D) with Cas9 yielded consistent but more pronounced effects.
evidence: This is supported by the Cas9 knockout data in Figure 3D.

claim: DNMT3A/TET2 KD or KO show expected effects on CRP promoter methylation.
source: Importantly, DNMT3A/TET2 KD or KO showed expected effects on CRP promoter methylation and on their own expression (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2) without upregulating TFs critical to CRP induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the bisulfite sequencing data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DNMT3A/TET2 KD or KO do not upregulate TFs critical to CRP induction.
source: Importantly, DNMT3A/TET2 KD or KO showed expected effects on CRP promoter methylation and on their own expression (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2) without upregulating TFs critical to CRP induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the qPCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Overexpression of DNMT3A reduces CRP expression.
source: On the other hand, the overexpression of DNMT3A reduced, while the overexpression of TET2 enhanced CRP expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the overexpression data in Figure 3E.

claim: Overexpression of TET2 enhances CRP expression.
source: On the other hand, the overexpression of DNMT3A reduced, while the overexpression of TET2 enhanced CRP expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the overexpression data in Figure 3E.

claim: DNMT3A is a negative regulator of CRP expression.
source: These results together identify DNMT3A and TET2 as the negative and positive regulators of CRP expression, respectively, thus reinforcing the notion that CRP expression is causally determined by promoter methylation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figure 3.

claim: TET2 is a positive regulator of CRP expression.
source: These results together identify DNMT3A and TET2 as the negative and positive regulators of CRP expression, respectively, thus reinforcing the notion that CRP expression is causally determined by promoter methylation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figure 3.

claim: Enforced methylation of CRP promoter by DNMT3A-dCas9 reduces the expression of CRP but not SAA or SAP.
source: Enforced methylation of CRP promoter by DNMT3A-dCas9 reduced the expression of CRP in Hep3B cells, but showed little effect on that of serum amyloid A (SAA, another major human APR) and serum amyloid P component (SAP, a paralog of CRP) (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by the dCas9-DNMT3A targeting data in Figure 3F.

claim: Enforced demethylation of CRP promoter by TET2-dCas9 selectively enhances the expression of CRP.
source: By contrast, enforced demethylation of CRP promoter by TET2-dCas9 only selectively enhanced the expression of CRP (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by the dCas9-TET2 targeting data in Figure 3G.

claim: DNMT3A and TET2-tuned methylation status of CRP promoter constitutes a key part of the regulatory mechanism that causally determines the expression.
source: We thus conclude that DNMT3A and TET2-tuned methylation status of CRP promoter constitutes a key part of the regulatory mechanism that causally determines the expression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: IL-6 and IL-1β-induced demethylation of CRP promoter is paralleled by markedly enhanced recruitment of STAT3, NF-κB p50 and C/EBP-β.
source: Indeed, IL-6 and IL-1β-induced demethylation of CRP promoter (Figure 1G) was paralleled by markedly enhanced recruitment of STAT3, NF-κB p50 and C/EBP-β (Figure 4A; Singh et al., 2007; Young et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP data in Figure 4A.

claim: In vitro methylation substantially reduces the recruitment of STAT3, NF-κB p50 and C/EBP-β to vectors containing CRP promoter.
source: Moreover, in vitro methylation substantially reduced the recruitment of those TFs to vectors containing CRP promoter after transfection into Hep3B cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP data in Figure 4B.

claim: The −53CpG is at the binding sites of p50/C/EBP-β.
source: The −53CpG and −108CpG are at the binding sites of p50/C/EBP-β, and STAT3, respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the schematic diagram in Figure 1A.

claim: The −108CpG is at the binding site of STAT3.
source: The −53CpG and −108CpG are at the binding sites of p50/C/EBP-β, and STAT3, respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the schematic diagram in Figure 1A.

claim: Site-specific methylation of −53CpG selectively prevents the recruitment of p50 and C/EBP-β to CRP promoter.
source: Accordingly, site-specific methylation of −53CpG selectively prevented the recruitment of p50 and C/EBP-β to CRP promoter, while site-specific methylation of −108CpG only inhibited the recruitment of STAT3 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the site-specific methylation ChIP data in Figure 4C.

claim: Site-specific methylation of −108CpG inhibits the recruitment of STAT3 to CRP promoter.
source: Accordingly, site-specific methylation of −53CpG selectively prevented the recruitment of p50 and C/EBP-β to CRP promoter, while site-specific methylation of −108CpG only inhibited the recruitment of STAT3 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the site-specific methylation ChIP data in Figure 4C.

claim: CpG motifs at TF binding sites act as rheostats with their methylation turning down the recruitment of critical TFs.
source: These CpG motifs at TF binding sites may thus act as rheostats with their methylation turning down the recruitment of critical TFs, resulting in reduced expression.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data in Figure 4.

claim: IL-6 and IL-1β induce two waves of CRP expression: the first wave lasts from 0 to 6 hr yielding the minor peak, while the second lasts from 12 to 24 hr yielding the major peak.
source: IL-6 and IL-1β induced two waves of CRP expression: the first wave lasted from 0 to 6 hr yielding the minor peak, while the second lasted from 12 to 24 hr yielding the major peak (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the time course data in Figure 5A.

claim: The recruitment of STAT3 to CRP promoter occurs during the first wave and saturates at 3 hr before the minor peak.
source: The recruitment of STAT3 occurred during the first wave and saturated at 3 hr before the minor peak (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP time course data in Figure 5B.

claim: The recruitment of p50 to CRP promoter is more evident during the time lag between the two waves.
source: By contrast, the recruitment of p50 was more evident during the time lag between the two waves (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP time course data in Figure 5C.

claim: The recruitment of C/EBP-β to CRP promoter steadily rises till 12 hr.
source: The recruitment of C/EBP-β, whose action depends on p50 (Cha-Molstad et al., 2000; Kramer et al., 2008; Agrawal et al., 2001), however, steadily rose till 12 hr (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP time course data in Figure 5D.

claim: The action of C/EBP-β depends on p50.
source: The recruitment of C/EBP-β, whose action depends on p50 (Cha-Molstad et al., 2000; Kramer et al., 2008; Agrawal et al., 2001), however, steadily rose till 12 hr (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The first wave of induced CRP expression is driven by early recruited STAT3.
source: These would suggest that the first wave of induced CRP expression is driven by early recruited STAT3, which licenses the late recruitment of p50 that synergizes with C/EBP-β to drive the second wave.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the time course data in Figure 5A-D.

claim: STAT3 licenses the late recruitment of p50 that synergizes with C/EBP-β to drive the second wave of CRP induction.
source: These would suggest that the first wave of induced CRP expression is driven by early recruited STAT3, which licenses the late recruitment of p50 that synergizes with C/EBP-β to drive the second wave.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the time course data in Figure 5A-D.

claim: STAT3 is the pioneer TF that binds methylated CRP promoter to initiate induction and prime demethylation.
source: As such, STAT3 is likely the pioneer TF that binds methylated CRP promoter to initiates induction and primes demethylation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data showing STAT3 can bind methylated promoter (Figure 5B in TET2 KO cells).

claim: STAT3 is the only TF showing appreciable early recruitment to CRP promoter upon enforced DNA methylation by TET2 KO.
source: In line with the above suggestion, STAT3 was the only TF showing appreciable early recruitment to CRP promoter upon enforced DNA methylation by TET2 KO (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP data in TET2 KO cells shown in Figures 5B-D.

claim: STAT3 can be recruited to CRP promoter even when heavily methylated.
source: This indicates that STAT3 can nevertheless be recruited to CRP promoter even when heavily methylated, consistent with the observations that vector binding of STAT3 was least sensitive to methylation (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP data in TET2 KO cells (Figure 5B) and the in vitro methylation data (Figure 4B and C).

claim: Vector binding of STAT3 is least sensitive to methylation compared to other TFs.
source: This indicates that STAT3 can nevertheless be recruited to CRP promoter even when heavily methylated, consistent with the observations that vector binding of STAT3 was least sensitive to methylation (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP data in Figure 4B and C.

claim: STAT3 can act largely independent of p50 and C/EBP-β to drive CRP induction, albeit with a markedly reduced amplitude.
source: This also indicates that STAT3 can act largely independent of p50 and C/EBP-β to drive CRP induction, albeit with a markedly reduced amplitude (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the CRP expression data in TET2 KO cells shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The sole activation of STAT3 in wildtype cells induces CRP expression to a level comparable to that of the minor peak.
source: Indeed, the sole activation of STAT3 in wildtype cells was able to induce CRP expression to a level comparable to that of the minor peak, whereas the sole activation of NF-κB was completely ineffective (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by the single cytokine treatment data in Figure 5E.

claim: The sole activation of NF-κB is completely ineffective in inducing CRP expression.
source: Indeed, the sole activation of STAT3 in wildtype cells was able to induce CRP expression to a level comparable to that of the minor peak, whereas the sole activation of NF-κB was completely ineffective (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by the single cytokine treatment data in Figure 5E.

claim: NF-κB inhibition at the induced state results in an even stronger methylation of CRP promoter.
source: Despite that, NF-κB inhibition (with intact STAT3) at the induced state resulted in an even stronger methylation of CRP promoter (Figure 5F) and a reversal of allelic imbalance (Figures 5G and 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the bisulfite sequencing data in Figure 5F.

claim: NF-κB inhibition at the induced state results in a reversal of allelic imbalance in CRP promoter methylation.
source: Despite that, NF-κB inhibition (with intact STAT3) at the induced state resulted in an even stronger methylation of CRP promoter (Figure 5F) and a reversal of allelic imbalance (Figures 5G and 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the allele-specific methylation data in Figure 5G.

claim: Promoter demethylation requires p50 that acts downstream of STAT3.
source: Therefore, promoter demethylation requires p50 that acts downstream of STAT3.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figures 5E-G.

claim: Enforced DNA demethylation by DNMT3A KO triples CRP expression during the entire course of induction.
source: Interestingly, enforced DNA demethylation by DNMT3A KO not only tripled CRP expression during the entire course of induction, but eliminated the time lag between the two waves (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the time course data in DNMT3A KO cells shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Enforced DNA demethylation by DNMT3A KO eliminates the time lag between the two waves of CRP induction.
source: Interestingly, enforced DNA demethylation by DNMT3A KO not only tripled CRP expression during the entire course of induction, but eliminated the time lag between the two waves (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the time course data in DNMT3A KO cells shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The augmented amplitude of CRP induction in DNMT3A KO cells can be explained by the enhanced recruitment of STAT3, p50, and C/EBP-β.
source: The augmented amplitude can be explained by the enhanced recruitment of the three TFs, while the altered dynamics may correspond to the shifted timing of p50 recruitment (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the ChIP data in DNMT3A KO cells shown in Figures 5B-D.

claim: The altered dynamics of CRP induction in DNMT3A KO cells may correspond to the shifted timing of p50 recruitment.
source: The augmented amplitude can be explained by the enhanced recruitment of the three TFs, while the altered dynamics may correspond to the shifted timing of p50 recruitment (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the ChIP data in DNMT3A KO cells shown in Figures 5B-D.

claim: p50 selectively recruited during the time lag between the two waves is responsible for promoter demethylation to prime the second wave.
source: As such, p50 selectively recruited during the time lag could be responsible for promoter demethylation to prime the second wave.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the time course data in Figures 5A-D.

claim: C/EBP-β is the major effector that responds to promoter demethylation.
source: Accordingly, C/EBP-β appears to be the major effector that responds to promoter demethylation: its overexpression did not demethylate CRP promoter (Figure 5H and I), but when combined with blockage of DNA methylation, it drove the resting expression of CRP to a level approaching to that induced by IL-6 and IL-1β (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figures 5H-K.

claim: C/EBP-β overexpression does not demethylate CRP promoter.
source: Accordingly, C/EBP-β appears to be the major effector that responds to promoter demethylation: its overexpression did not demethylate CRP promoter (Figure 5H and I), but when combined with blockage of DNA methylation, it drove the resting expression of CRP to a level approaching to that induced by IL-6 and IL-1β (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by the methylation data in Figure 5H and I.

claim: C/EBP-β overexpression combined with blockage of DNA methylation drives the resting expression of CRP to a level approaching that induced by IL-6 and IL-1β.
source: Accordingly, C/EBP-β appears to be the major effector that responds to promoter demethylation: its overexpression did not demethylate CRP promoter (Figure 5H and I), but when combined with blockage of DNA methylation, it drove the resting expression of CRP to a level approaching to that induced by IL-6 and IL-1β (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data in Figure 5J.

claim: C/EBP-β KO lowers the induced expression of CRP by ~70%.
source: C/EBP-β KO, however, lowered the induced expression of CRP by ~70% (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data in Figure 5K.

claim: TFs and promoter methylation dynamically orchestrate in a stepwise induction of CRP.
source: These together demonstrate a stepwise induction of CRP where TFs and promoter methylation dynamically orchestrate (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data in Figure 5.

claim: SAA behaves similarly as CRP in terms of expression and promoter methylation dynamics.
source: Indeed, SAA behaved similarly as CRP.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 6A and B showing similar patterns for SAA.

claim: Treating Hep3B cells with IL-6 and IL-1β results in a drastic increase in the expression of SAA.
source: Treating Hep3B cells with IL-6 and IL-1β resulted in a drastic increase in the expression of SAA (Figure 6A) and a reduction in methylation levels of its promoter (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data in Figure 6A.

claim: Treating Hep3B cells with IL-6 and IL-1β results in a reduction in methylation levels of SAA promoter.
source: Treating Hep3B cells with IL-6 and IL-1β resulted in a drastic increase in the expression of SAA (Figure 6A) and a reduction in methylation levels of its promoter (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the methylation data in Figure 6B.

claim: The expression and promoter methylation of SAA are quickly recovered following cytokine withdraw.
source: These were, however, quickly recovered following cytokine withdraw.
evidence: This is supported by the time course data in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Neither the expression nor the promoter methylation of SAP is affected by treatment or withdraw of IL-6 and IL-1β.
source: By contrast, neither the expression nor the promoter methylation of SAP was affected by treatment or withdraw of IL-6 and IL-1β (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 6A and C showing no changes for SAP.

claim: DNMT3A KO markedly enhances the induced expression of SAA.
source: Moreover, DNMT3A KO also markedly enhanced the induced expression of SAA, but barely affected that of SAP (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data in DNMT3A KO cells shown in Figure 6D.

claim: DNMT3A KO barely affects the induced expression of SAP.
source: Moreover, DNMT3A KO also markedly enhanced the induced expression of SAA, but barely affected that of SAP (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data in DNMT3A KO cells shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Reversible promoter methylation may be a general mechanism underlying the induction of APRs.
source: These results suggest that reversible promoter methylation may be a general mechanism underlies the induction of APRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 6 showing similar patterns for multiple APRs.

claim: The promoters of most mammalian genes contain a high frequency of CpGs termed CpG islands (CGIs) that are resistant to DNA methylation.
source: The promoters of most mammalian genes contain a high frequency (observed number/expected number >0.6) of CpGs termed CpG islands (CGIs) that are resistant to DNA methylation (Saxonov et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The CpG frequency of CRP promoter is exceptionally low (~0.23).
source: The CpG frequency of CRP promoter, however, is exceptionally low (~0.23).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the CRP promoter.

claim: A low CpG frequency appears to be a general feature of APR promoters.
source: Interestingly, a low CpG frequency appears to be general feature of APR promoters (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis in Figure 7A comparing APR promoters to other gene classes.

claim: Both the numbers and ratios of promoter CpG are significantly lower in APRs than in cytokines, housekeeping genes or all genes of HG19.
source: (A) Both the numbers and ratios of promoter CpG are significantly lower in APRs (n = 34) than in cytokines (n = 117), housekeeping genes (n = 425) or all genes of HG19 (n = 20180).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In Hep3B cells treated with IL-6 and IL-1β, strongly induced genes tend to manifest lower CpG ratios in their promoters.
source: In Hep3B cells treated with IL-6 and IL-1β, strongly induced genes tended to manifest lower CpG ratios in their promoters (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In livers of mice undergoing turpentine-induced acute inflammation, genes whose expression changed by over 2-fold exhibit lower promoter CpG densities.
source: Similar observations were also made in livers of mice undergoing turpentine-induced acute inflammation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by the mouse liver transcriptome and methylome analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Genes with CpG-poor promoters show significantly stronger changes in both expression and promoter methylation.
source: Importantly, genes with CpG-poor promoters showed significantly stronger changes in both expression and promoter methylation (Figure 7D and E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the genome-wide analysis shown in Figures 7D and E.

claim: Dynamic methylation may regulate the expression of highly inducible genes with CpG-poor promoters.
source: Therefore, dynamic methylation may also regulate the expression of highly inducible genes with CpG-poor promoters.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genome-wide analysis in Figure 7.

claim: At the induced state, the pioneered binding of STAT3 to CRP promoter in hepatocytes drives a minor wave of induction.
source: At the induced state, the pioneered binding of STAT3 to CRP promoter in hepatocytes drives a minor wave of induction, and further licenses the subsequent recruitment of NF-κB p50.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the data in Figure 5.

claim: STAT3 licenses the subsequent recruitment of NF-κB p50 to CRP promoter.
source: At the induced state, the pioneered binding of STAT3 to CRP promoter in hepatocytes drives a minor wave of induction, and further licenses the subsequent recruitment of NF-κB p50.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the data in Figure 5.

claim: STAT3 and NF-κB p50 work together to tip the balance of TET2 and DNMT3A at CRP promoter, leading to its demethylation.
source: The two TFs probably work together to tip the balance of TET2 and DNMT3A at CRP promoter, leading to its demethylation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data showing STAT3 and NF-κB involvement in demethylation.

claim: The methylated cytosine might be eventually removed by base excision repair mechanism.
source: As significant cell proliferation was not noted, the methylated cytosine might be eventually removed by base excision repair mechanism (Wu and Zhang, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of no cell proliferation and knowledge from the cited literature.

claim: The demethylated promoter enhances the recruitment of C/EBP-β to drive the major wave of CRP induction.
source: Consequently, the demethylated promoter enhances the recruitment of C/EBP-β to drive the major wave of CRP induction.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: During the recovery phase, the loss of activated STAT3 and p50 results in a rapid remethylation of CRP promoter and termination of induction.
source: During the recovery phase, however, the loss of activated STAT3 and p50 results in a rapid remethylation of CRP promoter and termination of induction.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the washout data in Figure 1G.

claim: At the resting state, the relatively hypomethylated promoter of CRP in the liver versus other tissues likely favors C/EBP-β recruitment, contributing to its tissue-specific, basal expression.
source: At the resting state, however, the relatively hypomethylated promoter of CRP in the liver versus other tissues likely favors C/EBP-β recruitment, contributing to its tissue-specific, basal expression.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the tissue-specific methylation data in Figures 1B-D.

claim: CRP is a putative pattern recognition receptor.
source: These may form the basis for CRP, a putative pattern recognition receptor (Du Clos, 2013; Bottazzi et al., 2010), to constitute an integral part of immune surveillance in both homeostasis and inflammation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DNA methylation is a relatively stable epigenetic modification.
source: In this regard, it is worth noting that DNA methylation is a relative stable epigenetic modification (Wu and Zhang, 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Dynamic changes in global or local DNA methylation status have been demonstrated in processes of development, aging and disease.
source: Though dynamic changes in global or local DNA methylation status have been demonstrated in processes of development, aging and disease, these (gradual) changes, once occurred, are largely persistent or irreversible (Wu and Zhang, 2014; Dor and Cedar, 2018; Luo et al., 2018; Halder et al., 2016; Sellars et al., 2015; Domcke et al., 2015; Flavahan et al., 2016; Dmitrijeva et al., 2018; Koch et al., 2018; Horvath and Raj, 2018) with its causality in determining gene expression even being questioned (Bestor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: DNA methylation changes in development, aging and disease, once occurred, are largely persistent or irreversible.
source: Though dynamic changes in global or local DNA methylation status have been demonstrated in processes of development, aging and disease, these (gradual) changes, once occurred, are largely persistent or irreversible (Wu and Zhang, 2014; Dor and Cedar, 2018; Luo et al., 2018; Halder et al., 2016; Sellars et al., 2015; Domcke et al., 2015; Flavahan et al., 2016; Dmitrijeva et al., 2018; Koch et al., 2018; Horvath and Raj, 2018) with its causality in determining gene expression even being questioned (Bestor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The causality of DNA methylation in determining gene expression has been questioned.
source: Though dynamic changes in global or local DNA methylation status have been demonstrated in processes of development, aging and disease, these (gradual) changes, once occurred, are largely persistent or irreversible (Wu and Zhang, 2014; Dor and Cedar, 2018; Luo et al., 2018; Halder et al., 2016; Sellars et al., 2015; Domcke et al., 2015; Flavahan et al., 2016; Dmitrijeva et al., 2018; Koch et al., 2018; Horvath and Raj, 2018) with its causality in determining gene expression even being questioned (Bestor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The expression of pS2 is regulated by rapid and reversible changes in DNA methylation.
source: There are, however, only rare cases where the expression of specific genes, such as pS2 (Métivier et al., 2008; Kangaspeska et al., 2008) and IL-10 (Hwang et al., 2018), is regulated by rapid and reversible changes in DNA methylation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The expression of IL-10 is regulated by rapid and reversible changes in DNA methylation.
source: There are, however, only rare cases where the expression of specific genes, such as pS2 (Métivier et al., 2008; Kangaspeska et al., 2008) and IL-10 (Hwang et al., 2018), is regulated by rapid and reversible changes in DNA methylation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The findings identify an important scenario in which reversible promoter methylation plays a critical role in determining the expression pattern of a class of proteins featured by CpG-poor promoters in response to inflammatory stimuli.
source: Our findings here identify an important scenario in which reversible promoter methylation plays a critical role in determining the expression pattern of a class of proteins featured by CpG-poor promoters in response to inflammatory stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's main findings.

claim: In mouse neurons activated by electroconvulsive stimulation, methylation changes were preferentially occurred in CpG-poor regions.
source: One study examined mouse neurons activated by electroconvulsive stimulation, and found that methylation changes were preferentially occurred in CpG-poor regions (Guo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In neurons activated by electroconvulsive stimulation, methylation changes in CpG-poor regions were modestly anticorrelated with gene expression.
source: Though promoters were underrepresented in these regions, their methylation changes were nevertheless modestly anticorrelated with gene expression (Guo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CpG content-dependent changes in DNA methylation were not observed in neurons activated by contextual learning.
source: Such CpG content-dependent changes in DNA methylation, however, were not observed in another study examining neurons activated by contextual learning (Halder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DNA methylation changes in human dendritic cells following infection rarely occurred at promoters.
source: Moreover, DNA methylation changes in human dendritic cells following infection rarely occurred at promoters (Pacis et al., 2019; Pacis et al., 2015), and were claimed to be a consequence of gene expression (Pacis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DNA methylation changes in human dendritic cells following infection were claimed to be a consequence of gene expression.
source: Moreover, DNA methylation changes in human dendritic cells following infection rarely occurred at promoters (Pacis et al., 2019; Pacis et al., 2015), and were claimed to be a consequence of gene expression (Pacis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The regulation of reversible methylation on inducible expression of genes with CpG-poor promoters may be context-dependent.
source: Those findings thus argue that the regulation of reversible methylation on inducible expression of genes with CpG-poor promoters may be context-dependent, and that rigorously controlled case study should be integrated into genome-wide investigation to conclude on causality.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the conflicting findings from different studies cited.

claim: Genes showing inducible expression in macrophages activated by endotoxin have been classified into nucleosome remodeling-independent genes with CpG-rich promoters and nucleosome remodeling-dependent genes with CpG-poor promoters.
source: Interestingly, genes showing inducible expression in macrophages activated by endotoxin have been classified into two groups: nucleosome remodeling-independent genes with CpG-rich promoters, and nucleosome remodeling-dependent genes with CpG-poor promoters (Ramirez-Carrozzi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Both nucleosome remodeling-independent and nucleosome remodeling-dependent genes in macrophages exhibit a single-wave kinetics of induction.
source: Despite their distinct requirements for SWI/SNF complexes, preassembled Pol II and new protein synthesis, both groups of genes exhibit a single-wave kinetics of induction (Ramirez-Carrozzi et al., 2009; Hargreaves et al., 2009; Ramirez-Carrozzi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CRP and probably other major APRs show a two-wave kinetics of induction with the second wave licensed by promoter demethylation.
source: This is in contrast with CRP and probably other major APRs, which show a two-wave kinetics of induction with the second wave licensed by promoter demethylation.
evidence: This is based on the data in Figure 5A showing two-wave kinetics.

claim: C/EBP-β promotes CRP expression by recruiting BRG1 via MKL1.
source: However, nucleosome remodeling might still act downstream in the second wave, as C/EBP-β has recently been shown to promote CRP expression by recruiting BRG1 via MKL1 (Fan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Most CpGs in mammalian promoters not associated with CGIs are usually methylated.
source: Despite that most CpGs in mammalian promoters not associated with CGIs are usually methylated (Wu and Zhang, 2014; Luo et al., 2018), TETs and DNMTs can nevertheless mediate active demethylation and de novo methylation, respectively.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TETs and DNMTs can mediate active demethylation and de novo methylation, respectively.
source: Despite that most CpGs in mammalian promoters not associated with CGIs are usually methylated (Wu and Zhang, 2014; Luo et al., 2018), TETs and DNMTs can nevertheless mediate active demethylation and de novo methylation, respectively.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: The methylation status of part of the genome may depend on the balance of TETs and DNMTs.
source: This indicates that the methylation status of part of the genome may depend on the balance of the two types of enzymes (Jones, 2012; Wu and Zhang, 2014; Dor and Cedar, 2018; Luo et al., 2018; Blattler and Farnham, 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cellular signaling able to tip the balance of TETs and DNMTs could represent a regulatory mechanism that finely and reversibly tunes the expression of certain genes in response to environmental cues.
source: Cellular signaling able to tip the balance of TETs and DNMTs could thus represent a regulatory mechanism that finely and reversibly tunes the expression of certain genes in response to environmental cues.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: TFs including NF-κB and EGR1 have been reported to evoke DNA demethylation in neurons.
source: Though the mechanism of TF-induced local demethylation is not fully understood (Luo et al., 2018), TFs including NF-κB and EGR1 have been reported to evoke DNA demethylation in neurons (Jarome et al., 2015) for example by recruiting TET1 (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TFs can evoke DNA demethylation by recruiting TET1.
source: Though the mechanism of TF-induced local demethylation is not fully understood (Luo et al., 2018), TFs including NF-κB and EGR1 have been reported to evoke DNA demethylation in neurons (Jarome et al., 2015) for example by recruiting TET1 (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.
